title: The Borrowed Antiquity: the Last Shah, the Coup That Gave Him the Throne, and the Exile That Could Not Find a Country
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Crown Prince of a Dynasty Seven Years Old

stops.name: Tehran, the birth of a soldier's son
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the house itself is not documented in standard sources, so the pin approximates central Tehran
stops.campa: A Persian Cossack Brigade officer named Reza Khan gets a son in Tehran, the second child and the first boy, and names him Mohammad Reza. The father commands other men's soldiers for a Qajar shah whose dynasty is running out of time, and holds no title beyond his rank. Standard sources fix the city and the day but not the house, so the boy is born in a town rather than in a room. Within seven years he will be crown prince of a dynasty his father has not yet founded, in a palace the reigning shah has not yet been made to leave.
suggested_refs: The Pahlavi family residence in Tehran, unlocated in standard sources

stops.name: Golestan Palace, a dynasty declared
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Reza Khan crowns himself in the Qajar palace, taking the throne from the family that built the room he is standing in and the name Pahlavi from a language of kings dead a thousand years. His six-year-old son is proclaimed crown prince the same year. The claim to Cyrus is settled here, by a soldier, in an afternoon, and everything the dynasty will later say about two and a half thousand years of unbroken monarchy is written backward from this room. The antiquity the boy inherits is younger than the boy.
suggested_refs: Golestan Palace, Tehran, coronation hall of both Pahlavi shahs

stops.name: Institut Le Rosey, the boy sent to Switzerland
stops.date_confidence: arrival attested to the day; the stay runs to 1936, five years, not the four sometimes given
stops.campa: The crown prince arrives at Institut Le Rosey on the seventh of September, the first Iranian royal to be schooled in Europe, and stays five years by Lake Geneva among the sons of the European aristocracy. His schoolfellows belong to houses that have been royal for centuries and have never had to say so. He learns French well enough to think in it, and will write his last book in it, dying, half a century later. He goes home in 1936, sixteen years old, to a father who has by then been shah for ten.
suggested_refs: Institut Le Rosey at Rolle, Vaud, school of the crown prince 1931-1936

stops.name: Tehran, the military academy
stops.date_confidence: enrolled 1936, graduated 1938; month and day of enrolment not given, defaulted to 01-01. One research lens compressed both years onto 1936 and is corrected here
stops.campa: He enters the military academy his father built, in a capital the same man is rebuilding by decree, and comes out of it after two years a second lieutenant. Reza Shah means the army to be the spine of the new state and means his son to be its officer before he is its king; the crown prince is put through ranks that a country without a tradition of them has just invented. He graduates in 1938. Three years later the army he has been trained to command will stand aside while foreign troops enter Tehran.
suggested_refs: The Madrasa Nezam military academy, Tehran, founded under Reza Shah

stops.name: Abdeen Palace, the marriage to Fawzia
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries Princess Fawzia, sister of King Farouk, at Abdeen Palace in Cairo, a match between the two Muslim monarchies most anxious to be seen as modern. A second banquet follows at Saadabad in Tehran in April, for the Iranian public. A daughter, Shahnaz, is born the next year, and no son after her. In 1948 he divorces her; she has already gone home to Egypt. Forty-one years later this city will take him in when no other will, and bury him near the tombs of the family whose daughter he sent back.
suggested_refs: Abdeen Palace, Cairo, and Saadabad Palace, Tehran, the two wedding venues of March and April 1939

stops.name: Baharestan, the oath before the Majlis
stops.date_confidence: the abdication is 16 September, the oath 17 September; one lens dated this entry to the abdication and is corrected. Pin inherited byte-identically from mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json, which places the Majlis at Baharestan; a verification pass proposed 35.6919, 51.4320 instead and the divergence is recorded in the report
stops.campa: Anglo-Soviet forces enter Iran, and Reza Shah, whose German sympathies the occupiers will not tolerate, abdicates on the sixteenth of September. The next day his son takes the oath before the Majlis at Baharestan and is shah at twenty-one, of a country he does not control, in a capital garrisoned by two foreign armies. Twenty years later, in a book published in London, he will write that the Allies thought it fitting he should be in control of affairs. Khomeini will quote the sentence back at him.
stops.quote: The Allies, after occupying Iran, thought it fitting that I should be in control of affairs, and they agreed to my accession to the throne.
stops.quote_source: Mission for My Country (London, 1961), quoted in Ruhollah Khomeini, 'The Crimes of the Shah', footnote 5; the 1961 first edition was not located, so the wording rests on Khomeini's transcription of his enemy
suggested_refs: The Baharestan Majlis building, Tehran, seat of parliament in 1941

stops.name: The Soviet Embassy, the Tehran Conference
stops.date_confidence: conference runs 28 November to 1 December 1943, attested; embassy coordinates approximate, the compound since rebuilt
stops.campa: Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin meet in the Soviet Embassy compound at the end of November to settle the war and what will follow it. The Shah is the host of the conference and is not at its table; three foreign powers arrange the future of his country inside his own capital, guarded by their own troops. He is twenty-four years old and has been shah for two years. Of the four heads of state in Tehran that week, he is the only one whose government has no say in what is decided there.
suggested_refs: The Soviet Embassy compound, Tehran, site of the November 1943 conference

stops.name: Johannesburg, the founder dies abroad
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not supplied by the research pool, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Reza Shah dies at Johannesburg, exiled by the powers that removed him first to Mauritius and then to South Africa, three years after the abdication and a hemisphere from the throne he invented. The body goes to Cairo, to the Al-Rifa'i Mosque, and lies there six years before Iran takes it back in 1950. Thirty-six years after that, his son will be buried in the same mosque, beside a marker with nothing under it. The dynasty is eighteen years old and has already buried its founder abroad.
suggested_refs: The Reza Shah memorial chamber at the Al-Rifa'i Mosque, Cairo, emptied in 1950

stops.name: Tehran University, five shots
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the chronology lens says 'grazed' where the geography lens says 'wounded in the face', a discrepancy left standing
stops.campa: A gunman with a press card and a camera fires five shots at the Shah during a ceremony at the University of Tehran. He is hit in the face and lives. The Tudeh Party is banned in the aftermath and the powers of the throne are widened against the parliament that has spent eight years reducing them. In November he flies to Washington for the first time and asks Truman for arms and money. It is his first sight of the country that will hand him back his throne four years later.
suggested_refs: The University of Tehran ceremonial grounds, site of the February 1949 attempt

stops.name: Marble Palace, the marriage to Soraya
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates corrected from a submitted pin roughly 2 km east of the palace, which recurred in three entries
stops.campa: He marries Soraya Esfandiary-Bakhtiary at the Marble Palace, three years after sending Fawzia home, and the court press sells the match as a love match rather than an arrangement. Seven years of it will end because she bears him no child, and he will say the decision is against his wishes. Eleven weeks after this wedding the Majlis confirms Mohammad Mosaddegh as prime minister of Iran, and the reign that has been a formality since the occupation becomes a contest between two men over one country's oil.
suggested_refs: The Marble Palace (Kakh-e Marmar), Imam Khomeini Street and Valiasr Street, Tehran

stops.name: Baharestan, the oil nationalized
stops.date_confidence: the Majlis confirmation of Mosaddegh on 28 April 1951 is attested in the atlas file; the nationalization of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company is carried as [R], general historical record not refetched this session
stops.campa: Mosaddegh, confirmed prime minister at Baharestan, nationalizes the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, and the argument between the throne and the parliament stops being about protocol. In July of the following year the Shah refuses him the War Ministry, and the refusal is reversed only after the streets rise in the Si-ye Tir days. Command of the armed forces is the whole question: the constitution gives it to the shah, and a prime minister who does not hold it governs a country whose army answers to somebody else.
suggested_refs: The Anglo-Iranian Oil Company nationalization acts of 1951 and the Si-ye Tir uprising of July 1952
sources: general historical record, not independently refetched this session

stops.name: Kelardasht, the firman signed on the Caspian
stops.date_confidence: the firman is signed 13 August 1953 and the signing precedes rather than follows the failure of Nassiri's mission; one lens reversed the causal order and placed the Shah at Ramsar rather than Kelardasht, and both errors are corrected. Kelardasht coordinates approximate
stops.campa: At his villa in the Caspian highlands at Kelardasht the Shah signs a firman dismissing his prime minister and naming General Fazlollah Zahedi in his place, then leaves the delivery to a colonel and waits by the sea. Britain wants the oil back and Washington has agreed to help take it; the decree is the one piece of the operation only he can supply, and the only part of it that is written down and signed. Three days pass between the signing and the knock on Mosaddegh's door, and in those three days the prime minister's people learn what is coming.
suggested_refs: The Shah's villa at Kelardasht, Mazandaran, where the dismissal firman was signed

stops.name: Kakh Street, Nassiri at the door with a firman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; pin inherited byte-identically from mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json
stops.campa: Colonel Nematollah Nassiri comes to the house on Kakh Street with the Shah's firman in his hand and is arrested at the door by soldiers loyal to the prime minister. The first coup collapses inside the hour. By morning the paper that was supposed to end Mosaddegh's government is evidence against the man who signed it. Three weeks earlier, on the other side of the world, Fidel Castro attacked the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba and failed too; only one of the two failures is followed by a second attempt with a foreign budget.
suggested_refs: Mosaddegh's house on Kakh Street, Tehran, and the firman of 13 August 1953

stops.name: Ramsar, the Shah leaves the country
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; pin inherited byte-identically from mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json. Ramsar is the transit airfield, not the residence
stops.campa: Learning what happened at Kakh Street, the Shah leaves Kelardasht at four in the morning, flies a small plane to the airfield at Ramsar and from there out of the country: Baghdad the same day, where King Faisal the Second lodges him in a government guest house, and Rome two days after that. He has reigned for twelve years and abandons the throne in twelve hours. Soraya goes with him. The luggage is packed for a holiday, because a holiday is what the radio in Tehran is calling it.
suggested_refs: Ramsar airfield, Mazandaran, and Al-Rashid air base, Baghdad, the two stops of 16 August 1953

stops.name: Rome, the hotel and the second attempt
stops.date_confidence: he remains in Baghdad until 18 August and reaches Rome that day, so the window is 18-22 August, not the 17-22 submitted. The Hotel Excelsior detail is [R]: the coup's own record does not name the hotel
stops.campa: He waits in a Rome hotel for four days while other men decide whether he is still a king, and tells reporters he knows his people love him. On the nineteenth, paid crowds and army units under General Zahedi shell Mosaddegh's house on Kakh Street, and the second attempt succeeds where the first collapsed. In Chile twenty years later the same method removes Salvador Allende and installs Augusto Pinochet. The Shah is in a hotel on the Via Veneto when he is told he has a country again.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Excelsior, Via Veneto, Rome, named by the press rather than by the coup record

stops.name: Mehrabad Airport, the throne handed back
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He lands at Mehrabad on the twenty-second to jubilant crowds, six days after leaving as a man with a suitcase. Zahedi is prime minister. Mosaddegh is tried by military tribunal in the autumn for treason against the Shah, sentenced in December to three years in solitary, and afterwards held on his own estate at Ahmadabad for life; the prosecution had asked for death. The throne is restored, and everybody in Tehran knows by whom. From this August the Shah rules rather than reigns.
suggested_refs: Mehrabad Airport, Tehran, arrival point of 22 August 1953 and departure point of 16 January 1979

stops.name: Marble Palace, the marriage to Farah
stops.date_confidence: the cited source gives 20 December 1959; the submitted entry gave 21 December. Sources genuinely conflict and the conflict is not resolved here, only recorded. Venue hedged: Wikipedia's Marble Palace article describes the palace as the site of the engagement
stops.campa: Soraya is divorced in 1958, childless, and eighteen months later he marries Farah Diba, an architecture student of twenty-one, in a ceremony the record places at the Marble Palace and elsewhere calls only their engagement. A son, Reza, is born within the year, and three more children after him. The dynastic problem that ended two marriages is solved at the third attempt, thirty-three years after a Cossack officer made the throne hereditary in his own family.
suggested_refs: The Marble Palace, Tehran, named variously as the site of the engagement and of the wedding
sources: general historical record for the 1958 divorce and the 1960 birth

stops.name: Tehran, the referendum on six points
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin is the atlas's canonical Tehran coordinate, the referendum having no single site
stops.campa: He puts six points to a national referendum: land reform, forests nationalized, state enterprises sold, workers given a share of profits, women given the vote, a literacy corps sent to the villages. The result is announced as 5,598,711 in favour and 4,115 against, with the opposition boycotting. He calls it the White Revolution. The six points go to the country and not to the Majlis, so the reform arrives as a gift of the crown rather than an act of a parliament.
stops.quote: I was convinced that God had ordained me to do certain things for the service of my nation.
stops.quote_source: The White Revolution (Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1966), page 16, page-cited via Wikiquote; the primary text was not fetched
suggested_refs: The White Revolution referendum of 26 January 1963 and its published returns

stops.name: Qom, the cleric arrested at three in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the hour. A submitted entry fused this arrest with the separate November 1964 arrest over the capitulations and sent him straight to Iraq; both errors are corrected here. Qom pin inherited byte-identically from michel_foucault.journey.json
stops.campa: On the third of June, at Ashura, a cleric in Qom denounces the White Revolution and the shah who decreed it. At three in the morning on the fifth he is arrested. Riots follow and are put down. Sixteen months later the same man attacks the immunity granted to American personnel in Iran, is arrested again in November 1964, and is deported. The Shah has removed Ruhollah Khomeini from the country and not from the argument, and the argument outlasts the removal by fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The Ashura sermon of 3 June 1963 at Qom and the capitulations speech of 26 October 1964

stops.name: Bursa, the town that keeps exiles
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the Najaf leg begins October 1965 and runs to 1978
stops.campa: Ruhollah Khomeini is set down in Bursa, in Anatolia, on the fourth of November, in a house under Turkish police watch, the Shah's answer to a cleric who has just denounced the capitulations agreement from the pulpit at Qom. Ankara will not keep him long; within a year Khomeini moves on to Najaf, where he teaches for thirteen years and writes the doctrine that will end the monarchy that exiled him. Bursa is only the first stop of a banishment that never brings the quiet the Shah intended.
suggested_refs: The house at Bursa where Khomeini was held from November 1964

stops.name: Marble Palace, the guardsman fires
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the submitted [R] tag is upgraded to [A] on event, date and framing, and only the coordinates were wrong
stops.campa: A conscript of the Imperial Guard named Reza Shamsabadi opens fire inside the palace grounds. The Shah is unhurt. It is the second attempt on his life in sixteen years and this one comes from inside the guard that exists to prevent them; afterwards the royal office is moved out of the Marble Palace to Sahebgharaniyeh, and SAVAK's surveillance is turned on the army. He is forty-five. The apparatus built to watch the country has begun to watch the room he is standing in.
suggested_refs: The Marble Palace grounds, Tehran, and the relocation of the royal office to Sahebgharaniyeh after April 1965

stops.name: Ahmadabad, the prisoner dies on his own land
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; pin inherited byte-identically from mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json
stops.campa: Mohammad Mosaddegh dies on his own land at Ahmadabad, eleven years into a house arrest that followed three years of solitary confinement, fourteen years after the coup that removed him. He has asked to be buried at Ibn Babuyeh among the men killed in the streets for him in 1952. The government refuses, and he is interred under the floor of his own dining room. The state that arranges this is the state he governed, and the grave it allows him is inside a private house the public cannot enter.
suggested_refs: The Mosaddegh house at Ahmadabad-e Mosaddeq and the refused burial at Ibn Babuyeh cemetery

stops.name: Golestan Palace, the crown at last
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is his forty-eighth birthday
stops.campa: Twenty-six years after taking the oath he crowns himself Shahanshah at Golestan, saying he waited until Iran was strong enough for the crown to mean something. He sets it on his own head and then crowns Farah as Shahbanu. His father crowned himself in this palace in 1926 with a claim four years old. The son crowns himself in it with a claim of two and a half thousand years, and both ceremonies are held in a hall the Qajars built for a dynasty the Pahlavis removed.
suggested_refs: The coronation of 26 October 1967 at Golestan Palace, forty-one years after the dynasty's first

stops.name: Niavaran Palace, the house of the reign
stops.date_confidence: designed 1958, completed 1967, occupied from 1968; month and day not attested, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates reconciled from two lenses that disagreed by 450 metres
stops.campa: The family moves into the new palace at Niavaran, on the high northern edge of the city where the air is cooler and the distance from Tehran can be measured in degrees. Farah's four children grow up in it; the fifth Pahlavi child, Shahnaz, is Fawzia's, born in 1940 and grown. It is the residence of the last eleven years of the reign, and it will be kept afterwards exactly as they leave it, the furniture where it stood, the rooms of a family that walked out for a holiday.
suggested_refs: The Niavaran Palace Complex, Tehran, occupied 1968-1979 and preserved thereafter

stops.name: Persepolis, the tent city
stops.date_confidence: celebrations run 12-16 October 1971, attested; note that giuseppe_tucci.journey.json pins Persepolis at 29.935, 52.891 for a different event and the two pins are left divergent
stops.campa: Fifty tent apartments of silk and French furniture rise on a hundred and sixty acres beside the ruins, built by a Paris decorating firm around a central fountain, with a Tent of Honor and a banqueting hall sixty-eight metres long. Kings and presidents come to eat in it, marking two thousand five hundred years of Persian monarchy. Beyond the perimeter is a country whose literacy corps is eight years old. The atlas already holds Cyrus at Pasargadae, north of this table, and the claim being made here is that the line between them is unbroken.
suggested_refs: The Maison Jansen tent city at Persepolis, October 1971
sources: Wikipedia, '2,500 year celebration of the Persian Empire'

stops.name: Shahyad Aryamehr, eight thousand blocks of marble
stops.date_confidence: inauguration attested to the day; opened to the public 14 January 1972
stops.campa: Four days into the celebrations he opens a gateway at the western entrance of Tehran: eight thousand blocks of white Isfahan marble on a design by the architect Hossein Amanat, chosen by competition in 1966, built for about six million dollars. It is called Shahyad Aryamehr, the Shah's Memorial, Light of the Aryans. A museum sits beneath it. Within eight years the arch will still stand at the edge of the city, unaltered, and the two words naming him will be gone from it.
suggested_refs: The Shahyad Aryamehr tower, Tehran, inaugurated 16 October 1971

stops.name: Tehran, two French physicians
stops.date_confidence: May 1974 attested to the month; day not given, defaulted to 01. The disease is chronic lymphocytic leukemia, later described as Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia; the 'non-Hodgkin lymphoma' of the submitted entry is a retrospective gloss and is corrected
stops.campa: Two French haematologists, Jean Bernard and Georges Flandrin, examine him in Tehran in May and find chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The finding is kept from the Iranian public, from his own government, and reportedly from the American intelligence service that is advising him on everything else. He is fifty-four and has ruled for thirty-three years. The following year he dissolves the parties and makes Rastakhiz the only legal one, so that a country with a dying king also has no opposition with an address.
stops.quote: Thank God we in Iran have neither the desire nor the need to suffer from democracy.
stops.quote_source: Attributed remark recorded in Asadollah Alam, The Shah and I: The Confidential Diary of Iran's Royal Court, 1969-1977 (1991), page 233; the diary text was not fetched, only a secondary citation of the page
suggested_refs: The May 1974 examination by Jean Bernard and Georges Flandrin; the 1975 founding of the Rastakhiz Party
sources: general historical record, verified against the corrected diagnosis; Wikipedia, 'Death and state funeral of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi'

stops.name: Niavaran Palace, the island of stability
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: At a New Year's Eve dinner at Niavaran the President of the United States raises his glass and calls Iran an island of stability in one of the more troubled areas of the world, and credits the Shah's leadership and the admiration of his people for it. Six weeks earlier, on the South Lawn in Washington, tear gas fired at demonstrators had drifted across the arrival ceremony and both heads of state were photographed wiping their eyes. Thirteen months from this dinner the Shah leaves Iran.
stops.quote: Let the dog bark; the moon shall beam on.
stops.quote_source: Attributed remark, per Gholam R. Afkhami, The Life and Times of the Shah (2009), page 261; a secondhand attribution in a biography, not the Shah's own written or recorded words
suggested_refs: Carter's toast at Niavaran, 31 December 1977, and the tear-gassed arrival ceremony of 15 November 1977

stops.name: Jaleh Square, Black Friday
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; no research lens supplied a coordinate for Jaleh Square itself, so the atlas's canonical Tehran pin is used
stops.campa: Martial law is declared in the morning and by the afternoon soldiers are firing into a crowd at Jaleh Square. The day is remembered as Black Friday. Michel Foucault arrives in Tehran within days to report the demonstrations for Corriere della Sera, goes on to Qom to be received by clerics who explain to him a government founded on religion, and writes that a whole people prefers death to the Shah. The Shah is at Niavaran. From this month the demonstrations do not stop.
suggested_refs: Jaleh Square, Tehran, 8 September 1978; Foucault's Corriere della Sera dispatches from Tehran and Qom

stops.name: Mehrabad Airport, the vacation
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He leaves from the same airport he returned to in August 1953. The official word is that the Shah is going on vacation. Prime Minister Bakhtiar kisses his hand on the tarmac and the Shah weeps in front of the cameras. Farah goes with him. He is fifty-nine, has been shah for thirty-seven years, twenty-six of them since the coup handed the throne back, and this is the second time he has flown out of Mehrabad with the country in the street behind him. There is no third return.
stops.quote: A king, when he doesn't have to account to anyone...is inevitably very much alone.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to an interview with Oriana Fallaci, published in the Chicago Tribune, 30 December 1973; attribution via Wikiquote, the original interview text not fetched
suggested_refs: The departure from Mehrabad, 16 January 1979

stops.name: Neauphle-le-Chateau, the garden that governs Iran
stops.date_confidence: the Paris pin is inherited byte-identically from michel_foucault.journey.json and mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json, which use the canonical Paris coordinate for the Neauphle-le-Chateau garden; the date here is the day of the Shah's departure, with Khomeini's return on 1 February
stops.campa: For four months the revolution has been directed from a rented garden in a village outside Paris, by telephone and by cassettes flown to Tehran and copied in bazaar back rooms. The man in the garden was put on the road out of Iran by the Shah in 1964 and has been fourteen years in exile, thirteen of them at Najaf and four months here. On the first of February, two weeks after the Shah's aircraft leaves Mehrabad, an Air France charter brings Khomeini back to Tehran through crowds counted in the millions.
stops.quote: You think that Mr Khomeini, [an] uneducated person ... could have planned all this? Masterminded all this, set up all the organization? I know that one man alone could not have done it ... I know that a tremendous amount of money was spent ... I know that top experts in propaganda were used to show us like tyrants and monsters, and the other side as democratic liberal revolutionaries who want to save the country.
stops.quote_source: Interview with David Frost, 'The Shah Speaks,' January 1980, per Wikiquote; the bracketed insertion and the ellipses are the source's own. The video was not fetched
suggested_refs: The rented house and garden at Neauphle-le-Chateau, Yvelines, October 1978 to February 1979

stops.name: Tehran, the throne the coup saved is taken
stops.date_confidence: sources place the constitutional end of the monarchy on 11 February 1979; the flight itself was 16 January, and mohammad_mosaddegh.journey.json dates the final departure to 11 February. The two datings are left standing side by side rather than merged
stops.campa: The army declares itself neutral and the monarchy ends. Sources place the constitutional end of the Pahlavi state on the eleventh of February, twenty-six years after Operation Ajax put the throne back under a man who had abandoned it. What replaces it will refuse Mosaddegh too: at Ahmadabad the villagers name their school for him during the revolution, and Khomeini denounces him, and the school is renamed for Khomeini. The Shah put him under his own dining-room floor, and the republic takes his name off a village school.
suggested_refs: The declaration of army neutrality and the collapse of the Bakhtiar government, February 1979

stops.name: Tehran, Shahyad becomes Azadi
stops.date_confidence: the source gives the year 1979 only; pinned here to the revolution's triumph, when the honorific fell with the dynasty. The exact renaming date is not attested
stops.campa: The arch at the western gate loses two words. Shahyad Aryamehr becomes Azadi, Freedom, and the eight thousand blocks of Isfahan marble stand exactly where they stood, unaltered, beneath a name that means the opposite of the one they were built to carry. The museum in the basement keeps its collection of Susa artifacts and its section on photography. Thirty years later the crowds of the 2009 election protests fill the square underneath, photographed against a gateway a shah put there.
suggested_refs: The Azadi Tower, Tehran, renamed after the 1979 revolution; the Azadi Museum in its basement

stops.name: Persepolis, the tents looted
stops.date_confidence: the source dates the looting to 1979 and places it in the aftermath of the revolution; month not attested, set after February and flagged as such
stops.campa: The tent city is stripped. The silk, the fittings, the furniture ordered from a Paris firm for one week in October 1971, all of it goes; what stays is the iron skeleton of the tent frames and the access roads, unmarked and open to anyone who walks in. In 2005 the government of the Islamic Republic is reported to be considering a reconstruction for tourism. The ruins the celebration was staged beside are older than the dynasty that borrowed them by two and a half thousand years, and they are still there.
suggested_refs: The surviving tent-frame rods and access roads at Persepolis
sources: Wikipedia, '2,500 year celebration of the Persian Empire'

segments.name: The Exile That Could Not Find a Country

stops.name: Aswan, Sadat receives him
stops.date_confidence: tagged [R] in the research pool: the Aswan leg of 16-30 January 1979 rests on Wikipedia's 'Farah Pahlavi' rather than on a dedicated source
stops.campa: Anwar Sadat receives him at Aswan, the first stop of an exile that will run eighteen months through six countries and end back in Egypt. Sadat does it as a personal loyalty and it costs him in the Arab world. The Shah expects to be away for weeks; he travels with Farah, a household, and a diagnosis he has told almost nobody about. Forty years ago he married the sister of Egypt's king in Cairo. That dynasty is gone as well, and its tombs are in the mosque where he will be buried.
suggested_refs: The Egyptian presidential reception at Aswan, January 1979

stops.name: Marrakesh, the first refusal
stops.date_confidence: tagged [R]; the 30 January to 30 March window comes from Wikipedia's 'Farah Pahlavi'. The guest residence is not named in standard sources, so the pin is the city
stops.campa: King Hassan the Second takes him next, on the thirtieth of January, and keeps him until the thirtieth of March. The Islamic Republic is now a government with embassies, and it applies pressure; Morocco, which has its own clerics and its own street, asks him to leave rather than risk its relations. This is the first refusal. The five countries after it will each weigh the same thing Morocco weighed, which is not whether he is owed asylum but what granting it will cost at home.
suggested_refs: The Moroccan royal guest residence at Marrakesh, unnamed in standard sources

stops.name: Paradise Island, the visa not renewed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the stay runs to 10 June 1979
stops.campa: The Bahamas sell him a spring. He and Farah wait on Paradise Island among the hotels for some country to offer something permanent, and none does; when the tourist visas come up for renewal they are not renewed. He is a head of state with a fortune, thirty years of alliance with Washington and the decorations of most of the courts of Europe, and he is being processed as an overstaying visitor. The leukemia is progressing while the paperwork is refused.
stops.quote: As far as we are concerned, we are not the toys of any country, including the United States.
stops.quote_source: Meet the Press (NBC), 1973. Wikiquote dates it only to 1973; the '18 November' circulating with it is a scraping artifact from an adjacent citation to a 2007 MSNBC page, and is dropped
suggested_refs: The Bahamian residence on Paradise Island, spring 1979

stops.name: Cuernavaca, the summer villa
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the stay runs to 22 October 1979
stops.campa: Mexico grants a visa after David Rockefeller and Henry Kissinger press for it, and the family rents a villa outside Mexico City for the summer. The stay runs four months behind a wall and a guard detail. The same men will press for the next admission, and it is that one, into the United States for surgery, that brings the embassy in Tehran down on the heads of the people working inside it. Here that is still ahead: a sick man in a rented house in a country that has agreed to a visa and not to a future.
suggested_refs: The rented villa at Cuernavaca, Morelos, June to October 1979

stops.name: New York, the surgery and the embassy
stops.date_confidence: 22 October 1979 attested; the submitted 'mid-October' is corrected, and the tag rises from [R] to [A]. The embassy is seized 4 November, thirteen days later
stops.campa: He is admitted to the United States for treatment and operated on at the New York Hospital in Manhattan on the twenty-second of October. Thirteen days later students storm the American embassy in Tehran and demand that he be handed back. He never is. In December, discharged and too dangerous to keep in a city, he is moved to a military hospital at Lackland Air Force Base in Texas while Washington searches for a government, any government, willing to take the man it spent twenty-six years underwriting.
suggested_refs: New York Hospital-Cornell Medical Center, October 1979; Lackland Air Force Base, San Antonio, December 1979

stops.name: Contadora Island, the general's island
stops.date_confidence: December 1979 to March 1980 attested to the month; day not given, defaulted to 01. The Lackland stay of the same month is folded into the preceding stop
stops.campa: General Torrijos puts him on a resort island in the Gulf of Panama, and for three months the Shah lives on Contadora while Tehran files extradition requests that Panama declines to pursue. He is sixty. Panama is the sixth country to house him in eleven months, and none of the six has offered him a year. His illness now needs surgery no island clinic can do. In March he asks Sadat, the one man who offered before anybody else did, whether the offer still stands.
suggested_refs: The Contadora Island residence, Panama, December 1979 to March 1980

stops.name: Koubbeh Palace, Cairo, the last asylum
stops.date_confidence: March 1980 attested to the month, day not given, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are Koubbeh Palace: one lens pinned Cairo in the Heliopolis area and another downtown, and neither matched the residence named
stops.campa: Sadat grants asylum a second time, over strong criticism at home, and gives him Koubbeh Palace, fourteen months after Aswan. Here he undergoes a splenectomy and further treatment, and here, in French, dying, he writes the book published later that year as Answer to History, in which the crimes of SAVAK are laid at the door of his prime minister Amir Abbas Hoveyda. Ervand Abrahamian calls the result the ramblings of a paranoid; Martin Kramer calls it the Shah at his very worst.
stops.quote: One of my chief "crimes" then, was to have wanted Iran to move from the oil age into the atomic age before it was too late.
stops.quote_source: The Shah's Story / Answer to History (Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1980), page 68. A circulating shortened version drops the word 'then,' and the closing phrase without ellipses; the full sentence is restored here. Page-level citation via Wikiquote only
suggested_refs: Koubbeh Palace, Cairo, residence of the exile from March 1980; Reponse a l'histoire, written there in French

stops.name: Maadi Military Hospital, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the hospital is named as a Cairo military hospital, with some sources naming Maadi specifically
stops.campa: He dies at the military hospital at Maadi on the twenty-seventh of July, sixty years old. The immediate cause is recorded as infections following the splenectomy rather than the cancer itself, six years and two months after two French doctors found the leukemia in a room in Tehran. He has been out of Iran for eighteen months and has held no office for seventeen of them. Farah is with him. Of the states that received him in those eighteen months, one has agreed to keep him.
stops.quote: A sovereign is not a dictator. There is an alliance between him and his people which he cannot break.
stops.quote_source: The Shah's Story / Answer to History (Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1980), page 182, page-cited via Wikiquote; the memoir itself was not independently fetched
suggested_refs: The Maadi military hospital, Cairo, 27 July 1980
sources: Wikipedia, 'Death and state funeral of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi'

stops.name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque, the state funeral
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; coordinates corrected from two lenses that placed the mosque 700 and 900 metres west of Salah al-Din Square
stops.campa: Sadat gives him a state funeral in the mosque of the Egyptian royal dead. Richard Nixon attends, and Constantine, the exiled king of Greece. He is laid near the tombs of the Muhammad Ali dynasty, near Farouk, whose sister he married and sent home. His own father lay in this mosque from 1944 until 1950, when Iran took the body back; what is left in that chamber is a marker with nobody beneath it. The son is buried beside his father's absence, in a country neither of them ruled.
stops.quote: A crown, a throne could not be based on the not too very solid foundation of blood.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a filmed interview with David Frost, 'The Shah Speaks,' January 1980; attribution via Wikiquote, the video and transcript not fetched
suggested_refs: The Al-Rifa'i Mosque, Salah al-Din Square, Cairo, beside the Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan
sources: Wikipedia, 'Death and state funeral of Mohammad Reza Pahlavi'

stops.name: Niavaran Palace, the rooms kept as they were
stops.date_confidence: the private library section is reported opened to the public in 1994; that date and the architect attribution are [R], not present in the Wikipedia article cited for the palace itself. Month and day not given, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The palace is kept. The republic that abolished the dynasty preserves its last residence exactly as the family left it in January 1979, the interiors unaltered, and opens the private library section to the public in 1994. Visitors walk through the room where Carter raised his glass. No source consulted describes the condition of the grave in Cairo, or who maintains it, or whether anyone comes: the palace of the Shah is documented and the tomb of the Shah is not.

stops.name: Iran, the name in the street
stops.date_confidence: the 2017-18 unrest is attested; later rounds reported into 2025-26. Month and day not given, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: In the unrest of 2017 and 2018 some crowds chant for the return of Reza Shah, the Cossack officer, and are shouted down inside the same crowds. In later rounds, reported into 2025 and 2026, the name that carries is Reza Pahlavi, the son, who declared himself Reza Shah the Second in 1980 and has spent four decades proposing a referendum rather than a restoration. No accession has occurred and the title is recognized nowhere. Both names belong to a dynasty that ended before most of the people chanting them were born.
stops.quote: At no time during my reign were there more than 3,164 so-called political prisoners, most of whom were terrorists.
stops.quote_source: The Shah's Story / Answer to History (Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, 1980), pages 198-199, page-cited via Wikiquote. A contested figure, disputed by human-rights reporting of the era and not checked against the memoir text
